newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West wins criticism of Cuba by U.N. rights body.
newsitem.headline: West wins criticism of Cuba by U.N. rights body.

text.p: The United States, backed by other Western countries, on Wednesday won condemnation of Cuba in the United Nations Human Rights Commission but the vote showed a drop in support for the annual exercise.
A total of 19 countries in the 53-member body voted for a U.S.-drafted resolution, one less than in 1996, and 10 countries, five more than last year said no, while 24 abstained against 28 last time.

Before the vote, U.S. delegation chief Nancy Rubin accused the administration of President Fidel Castro of denying the Cuban people fundamental freedoms, harassing pro-democracy activists and controlling the free flow of information.

But Havana's ambassador Carlos Amat Flores told the Commission in a fiery speech before the vote that the resolution was "part and parcel of the hostile policy of the United States waged against Cuba for the past 37 years."

Diplomats said the outcome, although partly a result of changes in the Commission's membership, reflected a growing feeling among developing countries that they were being asked to endorse the U.S. position in its long-running row with Cuba.

Western countries, including members of the European Union which supports a "constructive dialogue" with Havana on rights issues, and Japan, maintained their backing for the United States which argues Cuba is a major rights violator.

The resolution, based on a report by U.N. investigator and Swedish jurist Johan Groth who has never been allowed to visit the communist-ruled island, expressed deep regret at "numerous reports of violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms."
It called on Havana to release "the numerous persons detained for activities of a political nature" and "to ensure that workers' rights are safeguarded...."

Before the voting, India, Indonesia and Algeria all told the Commission that Washington -- which has had no relations with Havana since soon after the 1959 revolution and and has maintained an economic embargo against the island for nearly four decades -- should talk directly to Cuba.

The Indian representative, who voted against, suggested the annual tabling of the resolution was "losing its utility" and seemed only to worsen the already deep hostility between Cuba and the United States.

Even Chile, which voted for the resolution, complained that it incorporated a bilateral problem -- the downing of two planes flown by Cuban exiles near the island in early 1996 -- which was already covered last year and whose repetition "does not serve the interests of human rights."

The plane incident led to the signing by President Bill Clinton of a measure known as the Helms-Burton law -- widely condemned by U.S. trading partners in Latin America and Europe -- aimed at limiting foreign investment in Cuba.
U.S. delegate Rubin said the Castro government "continues to swim against the tide of history" and that the Cuban people "want to enjoy civic rights and democracy."

But Cuba's Amat accused the United States of using "unscrupulous blackmail" to maintain backing for the resolution and declared his country "will continue to develop the social, economic and political path it has drawn up for itself....
"We will not have a fresh conquest of Cuba....which is writing its own history with dignity and pride," he said.
